Uniform Title: Jñānakārikā Secondary Title: Kaulajñānanirṇaya and Some Minor Texts of the School of Matsyendranātha Author: Matsyendranātha
Alternative name: Matsyendra;
Alternative name: Macchaghaṇḍapāda;
Editor: Bagchi, P. C.

Description: The source of this e-text is the *Calcutta Sanskrit Series* (No. 3), which contains the *Kaulajñānanirṇaya* and several minor texts of the school of Matsyendranātha, bundled together with the *Kaulajñānanirṇaya* and the *Kulānandatantra*. The printed volume also includes introductory material and summaries in English.

Place of publication: Calcutta Country of publication: India Title: Jñānakārikā
First Chapter. Om, salutations to Śiva. Salutations to the perfected beings (siddhas). Salutations to the feet of the illustrious Śaṅkara. Salutations to those whose principles are unimpeded.
Now, therefore, I shall fully proclaim the well-spoken *Jñānasarva*;
having set aside the *Kārikā* known as the *Śrījñāna*, I shall expound the *Jñānakārikā*.
The consciousness known as Kārikā is heard... O Vala! Now I shall explain the proper cause for yogins. (1.2)
And the path to liberation is free from all [dualities], devoid of all the sense faculties;
it is liberated from the five and the five, and is itself devoid of [all such categories]. || 1.3 ||
These gods [attained] that knowledge and liberation, remaining as they truly are;
it is free from all afflictions and is within the range of the senses. (1.4)
Likewise, the twelve-finger space (dvādaśānta) and similarly the state of peace (śānta);
the twelve-finger space consists of a hundred digits (kalā), yet it is devoid of phonemes and syllables. || 1.5 ||
He is the omniscient one, eternally peaceful, and free from all outflows;
he is Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Īśvara, and Śiva himself. (1.6)
The form of the embodiment exists as the unsurpassed cause, just as it is;
the form-body (rūpakāya) is eternally transcendent and free from mantra and tantra. (1.7)
That which is free from self and other, transcending all positions, and is the refuge...
[is the definition]. (1.8)
It is entirely free from all dualities, certain, and undisturbed;
whereas the mind of those whose consciousness is attached to sense objects is characterized by agitation. (1.9)
Then, deluded by the impurity of illusion, they wander through saṃsāra;
this is declared to be the determination of the duality of saṃsāra. 1/10
Now I shall speak of that liberation which is difficult to attain—that by the mere knowledge of which liberation occurs for yogins. (1.11)
Liberation is indeed free from all saṃsāra, undisturbed, certain, immovable, equanimous, beyond dualities, and tranquil. || 1/12 ||
There would be liberation for men, free from the state of duality;
it is mindless, devoid of thought—the supreme knowledge of the Kārikā. (1.13)
I have thus explained this distinction, which is the definitive determination of liberation itself:
[the state] completely free from all supports, and the mind likewise without support. (1.14)
Dharma has the mind as its support; it is known to be without support and bestowing liberation.
It is neither god nor goddess, nor anything else, being entirely free from both dharma and adharma. (1.15)
The substratum of dharma and adharma is declared to be the bondage of saṃsāra;
it is said that the substratum is bondage, and liberation is indeed without a substratum. (1.16)
When the mind is situated within its objects, free from duality and devoid of liberation, then reality—characterized by inconceivable liberation—becomes supportless. (1.17)

Then it wanders through saṃsāra, for that mind has no abode of certainty. O Goddess, O Knower of Wisdom, how is that mind to be known as motionless before it becomes restless, once it is freed from its various states? (1.18)
Thus ends the first chapter, the Section on Liberation, in the *Jñānakārikā*. Now, hereafter, I shall proclaim the knowledge that is difficult to obtain even in the three worlds.
The true essence of the Kārikās, arising from the lineage of Siddhanātha. (2.1)
Free from the sun and moon, devoid of gates and windows, [the yogi perceives] earth, water, as well as fire, wind, and space. (2.2)
It is heard from the Leader of Reality that the body arises from the five elements;
yet it is all-pervasive and peaceful, and no pervasion of it is found. (2.3)
Established directly in its pervasiveness, like clarified butter within milk—such is the reality described by the knowers of truth, a jewel of knowledge that is exceedingly difficult to obtain. (2.4)
The mind itself is free from self and other and is without support;
yet the duality that takes the mind as its support is without support and is the supreme medicine.
The mind is said to be of three kinds: the luminous (rāja), the passionate (tāmasa), and likewise the pure (sāttvika).
The third, however, is the *sāttvika* [nature], characterized by three qualities. || 2.6 ||

The tamasic [nature] is fickle and base; the rajasic is characterized by association with and attachment to passion; the third should be known as the sattvic, which is endowed with dharma and remains ever-steadfast. (2.7)
Now I shall describe the fourth, the mind itself, in particular:
it is forever free from the three qualities (guṇas) and has the characteristic of eternal liberation (nirvāṇa). || 2.8 ||

But that which is the supreme of the supreme fourth state, by means of which the mind is completely purified— that which transcends all subduing of the fires and transcends the senses, and is imperishable— (2.9).
The reality that is free from all mental constructs is always beyond practice;
it is liberated from the absence of mind, and this sign is the worldly reality. (2.10)
Non-existence that transcends cultivation, devoid of both mind and non-mind;
knowledge that is inconceivable from the outset of the mind, the determination of ineffable knowledge. (2.11)

Just as it has always been said that the mind is exceedingly fickle, so too it is said that a fickle state is [samsaric] existence, while an unshakable state is the characteristic of liberation. (2.12)
When the mind is joined with the intellect (citta), then it is known as flickering;
when the mind has transcended the intellect, it becomes certain and immovable. (2.13)
Free from all thought, it becomes immovable in non-existence;
yet the mind is not meditated upon through yoga, nor is it an achiever of characteristics. (2.14)
In that state, there would be no cessation, nor would there be the emptiness of the body;
it would not exist externally, internally, or in between, nor would it abide in the end, the beginning, or the middle. (2.15)
There is no fire, wind, space, earth, or the manifestation of water;
there is no intellect, nor ego, nor mind, nor the senses. (2.16)
Reality is neither mind nor non-mind; it is always established beyond thought.
That which is not thought is what must be known—one who knows this is a knower of the teaching of the [right] time. (2.17)
He who is the omniscient one free from thought, the supreme lord of meditative absorption—through him, the true nature of liberation, revealed through the secret divisions, is to be known. (2.18)

Knowledge that liberates one from the ocean of saṃsāra, whose sphere transcends conceptual construction, and which is always free from discursive thought, is declared to be the producer of gnosis. (2.19)
Volition and non-volition, as well as conceptualization and cultivation, [occur] within the spheres of the Moon, Sun, and Fire, through the placement of the support and the supported. (2.20)
Air, space, as well as the paths of movement, Brahmā, Rudra, and the other deities—all these are said to be conceptual constructions; otherwise, they are beyond conceptualization. (2.21)
But those joined with conceptual knowledge wander like a water-wheel;
how can they possess the perfect [state] which is devoid of the sequence of the Siddhas? (2.22)
Those who are stained by the cognition of the mind fall swiftly into saṃsāra;
but those who abide in the supreme state do not go into this saṃsāra. (2/23)
For him there is no going to hell, nor likewise any going to heaven;
he is liberated from the two snares that bind one to dharma and adharma. (2.24)
When the yogis have severed the binding of the two-fold noose with the sword of knowledge, where can their minds go once the blind noose has been cut? (2.25)
Bound by the double-noose of both dharma and adharma, beings fall and rise; bound by that noose, they experience the accumulation of their karma. (2.26)
Through dharma they enjoy heaven; through adharma, hell and the like.
Both dharma and adharma are that which bind the three worlds. (2.27)
When men quickly abandon both dharma and adharma, they are liberated;
for dharma and adharma are proclaimed to be two distinct categories. (2.28)
With a mind both external and internal, established in dharma and adharma, and possessing a true nature born of the inner self—thus does he abide for yogins alone. (2.29)
This [element] is subtle compared to worldly and terrestrial actions; moreover, the persistence of dharma and adharma always resides within the internal self. (2.30)
Dharma moves upward; its characteristic is non-duality and the absence of dharma.
When the exhaustion of both dharma and adharma has occurred, one is liberated from all worldly possessions. (2.31)
Having understood both dharma and adharma, one shall attain knowledge once again;
this investigation of dharma and adharma has been declared by the authors of the Jñānakārikās. (2.32)
Thus ends the second chapter, titled "An Investigation of Dharma and Adharma," in the *Jñānakārikā*.
Now begins the third chapter:
"I shall now explain the conduct that arises for yogins."
If that [self] were not consciousness, then consciousness would be devoid of knowledge. (3.1)

The state of consciousness joined with the mind is proclaimed as the nature of knowledge; when that consciousness experiences enjoyment, it is characterized by bondage, but when it is free from that, it possesses the characteristic of liberation. (3.2)
Consciousness, when joined with the mind and mental factors, is the eternal state;
it is contemplated through yoga by yogins and is devoid of noble conceptualization. (3.3)
That which is the characteristic of liberation for yogins, being free from the [ordinary] path, [is found] at a solitary linga, in a cremation ground, or at the confluences of rivers. (3.4)
The practitioner [should stay] in an empty house, a cave-dwelling, at the foot of a tree, in a crossroads, on the shore of the great ocean, or at a triple-pathway. (3.5)
Naked and with disheveled hair, their minds delighted by wine, the yogi wanders always alone, adorned with garlands. (3.6)
I shall now describe the *liṅga* which is known as the Kaulika;
that *liṅga*, which consists of the eightfold worship of dissolution (*laya-pūjā*), is indeed both the mobile and the immobile. (3.7)
Because it is the dissolution of all things, the Liṅga was joyfully fashioned by him;
this is the Kaulika Liṅga, which is not born of stone, gold, or silver. (3.8)
The bodily *liṅga* has been described as one and not two; it is declared to be the single *liṅga*. Now I shall describe to you the cremation ground (*śmaśāna*). 3/9.
When the body of all embodied beings shines, yet is joined with exhalation and inhalation, it is proclaimed as a cremation ground (śmaśāna). (3.10)
The movement of the vital breath flows perpetually both downward and upward.
When it moves upward, it becomes the Gaṅgā; and because it is established below, [the confluence occurs].
That which is the meeting of these two is proclaimed as *Na-met*.
If that reality which is bodiless is present within one's own body, [then... // 3.12 //
Having known it to be empty and stainless, one is liberated; of this there is no doubt.
I shall now declare the secret: within the secret, all that is moving and unmoving resides. (3.13)
The secret body is said to be perfumed by the mass of gnosis;
the yogi who abides in this secret dwelling has no conduct that can be described. (3.14)
The divine dwelling has been described; now hear likewise concerning the root of the tree.
It is said that the tree is the body, with the feet as its base and the hands as its branches. (3.15)
The mouth should have its roots above, supporting the tree at its base;
having understood the root of the tree, one should avoid the external tree. (3/16)
The root of the tree has been fully explained; now listen to the four [mantras]:
Jayā, Vijayā, Ajitā, and Aparājitā. (3.17)
Endowed with four powers and arising from the four measures, listen to the description of that divine fourfold [teaching] from the shore of the great ocean. (3.18)
The Bindu is that Supreme Power (Parāśakti), who is both situated on the shore and possesses a beautiful form;
she is eternally established within the Bindu, and the circle of the Bindu is situated on the shore. (3.19)
The yogi stands as one situated on the bank, and that very bank is thus proclaimed.
When, having abandoned the moon, he goes to the solar orb which is the support, [he attains liberation]. (3/20)
The numbering is incorrect;
when [the sun] departs from the solar orb and enters the lunar sphere, it remains eternally in the sky like the tide of the great ocean. (3.72)
At this time, it is declared that [the breath] is established within the self; the breath, colored by the mind, does not remain unstable when situated outside. (3.73)
It always carries the unstable current of all yogis;
it is the current, the movement, and indeed the coming and going once again. (3.74)
Just as at this time there is the occurrence of coming and going according to how things stand, so too, when there is no coming or going, no one is affected by passion. (3/75)
The world, remaining like the sky, should attain immovability through meditative cultivation;
having stood upon the shore of the great ocean, the ocean was then described. (3.76)
The state of being motionless and perfectly full is known as the great ocean;
this has been specifically taught as the reality of the true nature of the conduct of yogins. (3.77)
I shall now describe the "Great Ocean" (Mahodadhi), which consists of fifteen [categories], and how the qualities of sattva, rajas, and tamas abide in their state of unity. (3.78)
The *Jñānakārikā* explains that the triple-path (*tripatha*) is liberated according to the scriptures;
thus the triple-path has been fully described, and now I shall tell you about the naked one (*nagna*). (3.79)
Avidyā [is the consort] of the Lord of Sadhakas, who is naked and [appears at] the time of dissolution. Now hear about the naked gods whose hair is loose, as they have been described. (3.80)
Hair is said to be a bond that obstructs the path to liberation;
indeed, dharma alone is not sufficient, and this is especially true regarding bonds. (3.81)
When the yogi is liberated from the six, he is called "one with loosened hair" (muktakeśa). He is fully described as "one with loosened hair"; now hear about bliss (ānanda). (3.81)
The yogi who has reached the further shore of yoga is one who has abandoned the great shore;
he is proclaimed as a yogi [who partakes] of the divine nectar of the yoga of drinking. (3.83)
Endowed with these, the great yogi is said to be intoxicated by wine;
now hear about the garland of the one adorned with the remains of offerings, which is proclaimed as the bliss of wine. (3/84)
There is indeed color and the tip of the garland situated upon the thread of power;
this is declared to be the garland, which is another means for yogins.
Adorned with a garland of withered flowers, that yogi performs the yogic practice.
He who always speaks while wandering as a guest alone, and who wanders without a companion, that steadfast one is called "Ekākin" (the Solitary). // 3.86 //
The solitary one is indeed proclaimed [in] the *Milakārikā* treatise;
this is declared to be the conduct (*caryā*), O you who uphold knowledge, enter! (3.87)
Thus ends the third chapter, concerning the section on Conduct, as spoken by the one brought down by the venerable Jñānakārimahāmācchindranātha.
